content.text:
No, it isn't safe without a prefix, and the docs give you a fix: the `prefix` option.

- Use `@import "tailwindcss" prefix(tw);`. It prefixes the generated classes (`tw:text-red-500`) and the theme CSS variables (`--tw-color-red-500`). That is what keeps your variables from clashing with variables already on your users' sites. (`styling-with-utility-classes.mdx`, "Using the prefix option"; `upgrade-guide.mdx`, prefix section)
- Keep writing your `@theme` variables without the prefix (`--color-avocado-100`). The output adds it for you. (`upgrade-guide.mdx`, same section)
- Built-in utilities like `rounded-lg` keep working. They just become `tw:rounded-lg`, and their variables are prefixed too.
- I found nothing in these docs about stripping only the unused default variables. I didn't search for it beyond one query, so I can't say whether the docs cover it elsewhere.

No, it isn't safe without a prefix, and the docs give you a fix: the `prefix` option.

- Use `@import "tailwindcss" prefix(tw);`. It prefixes the generated classes (`tw:text-red-500`) and the theme CSS variables (`--tw-color-red-500`). That is what keeps your variables from clashing with variables already on your users' sites. (`styling-with-utility-classes.mdx`, "Using the prefix option"; `upgrade-guide.mdx`, prefix section)
- Keep writing your `@theme` variables without the prefix (`--color-avocado-100`). The output adds it for you. (`upgrade-guide.mdx`, same section)
- Built-in utilities like `rounded-lg` keep working. They just become `tw:rounded-lg`, and their variables are prefixed too.
- I found nothing in these docs about stripping only the unused default variables. I didn't search for it beyond one query, so I can't say whether the docs cover it elsewhere.
